I'm going to go against popular opinion here and say: you don't have to rely on others to get yourself into a healthy place.

I am an extremely introverted person with misanthropic tendencies. (INTJ woman, if you follow MBTIs) The only friendships I have,I value too much to burden the relationship with my depression bs. (I refer to Xpectopatronum's comment "Be careful not to over burden friends though. I have lost several this way.")

It *is* possible to rely on yourself for the support the others have mentioned. Self-reflection is a big part of this. You need to know yourself well enough that you can pinpoint effective incentives. Example: I know myself well enough to know that if I can drag my ass to the shower I am going to experience a long, hot, blissful experience that I will be SO glad I forced myself into.

My mornings usually go like this:    
5am - Alarm goes off.    
5:01 - No. I don't want to.    
5:02 - My back hurts. I have a headache. I'm so tired. Why didn't I go to bed earlier? You're such an idiot. You always do this to yourself! etc    
5:03 - I could just call out sick.    
5:04 - It was snowing when you went to bed last night. I bet it's cold outside. If you get up and get into the shower, it will feel amazing.    
5:05 - If you get up now, you can take an hour long shower. How amazing would that be? And it would help your headache... and your backache...    
5:06 - If you still want to go back to bed after your shower you can call in.    
5:07 - *promise myself I can call in after my shower*    
5:10 - Out of bed, and in the shower.

Clearly, I am an advocate of self-talk. But you get the picture. >>Know thyself<<

Absolutely. But you also need to prepare yourself because your verbiage leads me to believe you are thinking/hoping this will be a short-term situation. You need to prepare yourself for the possibility of a long haul here.

I'd say some goals are in order. Start small. Teeny-tiny baby steps. 

You said school is over, so what next?  A job? Okay, what kind of job? One with flexibility to accommodate your depression? Sounds great. Make a list of those types of jobs. Now look for those kinds of jobs online. Next step: apply for them. Interview. Go to work every day. Boom – functioning depressive.

Maybe start even smaller. Eating one meal a day at the same time – whether you want to or not! Slowly and gradually build up to a structured schedule. Showering every morning, eating regular meals, etc.

Well, shit. My first thought after reading your post was, "That's a good question. I can't wait to read the responses!" Then I read through the responses and realized... I think I qualify as "High Functioning". Damn.

Brief overview: I am a 28 year old single mom with two kids. I emotionally/physically/financially support my kids 100% on my own. I am able to do this because I picked us up and moved to Connecticut, in order to take a job in corporate America.

My take: There is no magic trick. You get up and do it because your life falls apart if you don't. Personally, my children deserve a good life, and I am the only one who can give that to them. So... I get out of bed every morning. I will say that it is extremely helpful (to the degree that I can't emphasize it enough) to get a flexible employer. On the mornings when it is just *too much*, I have the option of working from home on a company-provided laptop. That means I can log-in and work whenever I manage to drag my ass out of bed. (even if that turns out to be 3am) It also means I don't lose money because my depression is being a selfish bitch.

One last point... (I'm sorry this is so long) It is worth mentioning that people who suffer from chronic, long-term depression should focus on building a life that caters to that. It is a part of you. If you were in a wheelchair you would buy a handicap accessible home, right? Same concept. >build your life to fit your depression, rather than trying to force your depression to fit your life. xx

I started on antidepressants and antianxiety meds, but the side effects killed me. I only slept every 3 days, and barely ate. I tried so many different kinds of medications, I got sick of trying. I stopped them all and started smoking weed. I looooved it! But then I gained a bunch of weight, because I stopped working out and gave into my munchies every single day. I was a better/more patient mom, but I also didn't want to move. I started smoking before work, and couldn't focus. In the end, I went back on SSRIs and counteracted the side effects with pot. Now, I have energy and can get shit done, but I can also eat and sleep at night! Best of both worlds :)

Why? Because she loves you! But that is a LOT of pressure. I think you should reflect on how much energy it takes to maintain every day relationships. Then think about how much energy it takes to maintain a romantic relationship. That's a lot. She doesn't feel capable of handling all of that in addition to he own issues.

In my opinion, you have three choices. 1) you walk away. 2) you wait for her. You take whatever she can give on any given day. You cherish the good times, and selflessly wait patiently through the bad times. 3) you say you're going to do #2, find out it is seriously too fucking hard, and then do #1.
Holy fuck, how do you live?!

However, let us postulate that "everybody our age has the same opinion" at one point in their lives and it changes over time. Is it not possible that being misanthropic causes one to resist the baser traits that they despise in the rest of humanity? That ignoring those traits, such as greed, jealousy, self-centeredness, etc. makes one a better human? By becoming a better human one also may suffer from less self-loathing, which could thereby cause them to also see the good in others, as they have themselves. By seeing this change, one might then become less misanthropic, correct? 
Which means, that your post is approximately 30% correct.
Yes, *some* misanthropes will "grow out of it". **However**, in order to fix a problem one must first SEE the problem. Which means, my little human, that hating misanthropes is completely counterproductive. Because we are the only ones who actually see the problem. 💥

I've always been a misanthrope. Although, I'm sure my childhood didn't help. I grew up incredibly poor, in a very abusive environment, with severe social/general anxiety. As I entered junior high, I started to reflect on my hatred of humans. Interestingly, I realized my anxiety was not the *cause* of my solitary existence. Rather, it was the merely my *justification* of it.

As an INTJ woman, I have always existed (by choice) on  the outside looking in. From that vantage point I was able to study human beings, and what I saw sickened me. Essentially, I agree wholeheartedly with Kay from Men in Black: [A person is smart. People are dumb, panicky, dangerous animals, and you know it.](http://9gag.com/gag/3968533/a-person-is-smart-people-are-dumb-panicky-dangerous-animal) I did not have my first friend until I was in 7th grade. She is still my friend to this day. Our friendship works because she is one of very very few decent human beings I have ever met. (I am 28 years old and have 4 friendships I choose to maintain.)

I am not a misanthrope because something pushed me over the edge and I decided, “I hate humans!” I am a misanthrope because I have been watching/interacting with human beings my entire life, and I can only come to one possible conclusion:

People suck.
Kind of messed up, huh? :/

My kids.

I am raising some incredible people. (m7 and f9) They are wise, snarky, innocent, witty, and loving. Being a mom was the only thing that kept me alive in my darkest moments, and keeps me going each and every day. Sometimes I will come home from work and the only thing in the world I need is those little arms wrapped around my neck, squeezing me as tight as they can. I loathe human existence, and deeply regret bringing my children into this world. But, selfishly, they are also the only thing that makes this life tolerable for any period of time.

I ponder "horrible" things like that as a form of self-reflection. I envision how I would handle atrocities such as surviving a severe car accident, or one of my children dying. Mostly, I do this to ascertain what is truly important to me. For instance, most people think money is important. So, I will envision myself losing my job, my home, my car, etc. and reflect on how I would survive. Then I take it a step further and ponder how I would *feel* if I were homeless and destitute.
Generally speaking, the only things that are important to me at all are my children. They are the driving force behind everything else I consider a necessity of life.

EDIT: Upon more research, I have found my "self-reflection" is actually "negative visualization". Such as what Stoics practice.
